label: bm-bilayer-theory-verified
topic: The bilayer equations, each read in its original paper
summary: I read Timoshenko 1925 (J. Opt. Soc. Am. 11, 233-255, public-domain scan on the Internet Archive; the publisher site blocks automated fetches with a captcha, which I did not bypass), Stoney 1909 (Internet Archive scan), the Freund-Floro-Chason 1999 paper (open preprint, the companion of Freund 2000), Reyssat & Mahadevan 2009 (equation images), and Pezzulla et al. 2016 (arXiv). RESULT 1: Timoshenko's printed eq.(4) is the project's f(m,n) exactly, as are R&M eq.2.6 and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) with E replaced by E/(1-nu). Timoshenko 1925 does not state the ceiling 3/2 or the optimum m^2 n = 1; those are the project's own results, which I re-proved symbolically (3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(m^4n^2+4m^3n+6m^2n+4mn+1))) and by a 2.4-million-point grid. His own remark that the modulus ratio does not matter is limited to n between 1/2 and 2 at equal thickness (3 percent). RESULT 2 (assumptions): the formula is for a narrow strip, linear, perfectly bonded, plane sections, no Poisson ratio. For a wide plate Timoshenko himself replaces E by E/(1-nu) and f is unchanged (a sphere, while the sag is below about h/2). Plane-strain E/(1-nu^2) enters only after the plate flips to a cylinder, where the curvature is (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent); I derived this symbolically and it is confirmed by Pezzulla et al. (L+N = kappa_o(1+nu)) and by Alben's discrete model. Three independent criteria put the strip/plate boundary at a plate diameter of 2.0, 2.2 and 4.2 times sqrt(h/kappa). Stoney's 1909 equation is the thin-film limit of the same f. RESULT 3 (printed, wet, soft strips): the modulus ratio is a second-order risk at the optimum (a factor-2 error costs 2-3 percent of curvature; softening of the wet layer to 50 percent costs 2-3 percent), while large swelling strain, creep, the adhesive joint and anisotropic swelling are not covered by the theory and are not sized because no sources were found. Diffusion limits speed: tau ~ h^2/D (R&M), and for the only measured D of printable polymers (0.001-0.015 mm^2/h) my model gives a 90 percent curvature response at 0.72 a^2/D, 2-460 h for active layers of 0.2-0.8 mm. No diffusivity for any Formlabs resin exists in the sources found. RESULT 4 (honest gaps and one contradiction): Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 could not be read in the original (abstracts only), so their equations and critical values are not reproduced. Two Formlabs documents disagree on Flexible 80A water uptake (0.7 percent in an older cube-table row versus +8 percent mass in the V2 datasheet), so the project-record sentence that stock resins gain under 1 percent in water holds for the cube table but not for Flexible 80A V2.
lay_summary: A strip made of two layers bends when one layer swells more than the other, like a bimetal thermostat. The project's formula for how tightly it bends turns out to be the same one Timoshenko printed in 1925, so the maths is on solid ground. That formula is for a thin ribbon, though; a wide sheet behaves differently and rolls up about 30 to 50 percent tighter, in one direction only. It also says nothing about how fast the bending happens, and water creeps into ordinary plastics very slowly: a layer a few tenths of a millimetre thick can take hours to days, like a damp sponge that dries one thin layer at a time. Several things in a printed, soft, wet strip (big swelling, creep, the glue between layers) are outside the formula, and I could not find numbers for them. I also could not read three of the original papers in full, and two Formlabs documents disagree on how much one resin swells in water, most likely because they describe two versions of it.

glossary.plain: Two layers bonded together so that a difference in how they expand makes the strip curl.
How tightly something bends: one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
How stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch it by a given fraction.
How much a material gets thinner sideways when you stretch it lengthwise; about 0.3 to 0.5 for plastics and rubbers.
Two simplifications for a flat body: free to thin sideways (plane stress) or held from stretching sideways (plane strain); the stiff modulus then becomes E/(1-nu^2).
The stiffness of a sheet pulled equally in two directions, E/(1-nu).
The stretch a layer wants to have by itself (from swelling or heat) if nothing held it.
Same in every direction / different in different directions, like wood grain.
A ribbon that can only bend one way versus a sheet that must stretch if it tries to bend two ways at once.
The moment a wide sheet stops forming a bowl and flips to rolling up like a scroll.
The line inside a bent beam that is neither stretched nor squeezed.
How fast water spreads through a material; time to soak a layer of thickness h is about h squared divided by D.
Following the simple law that water moves from wet to dry in proportion to the difference.
A standard model of rubbery materials that stay accurate at large stretches.
Standard test recipes for fluid immersion, water absorption and tensile strength.
3D printing by light-curing liquid resin / by laser-fusing powder.
Technical data sheet from the manufacturer.
A computer program that does algebra exactly, used here to prove formulas.

findings.claim: PRINTED FORM. Timoshenko 1925 eq.(4), read from the page image (journal p.235): 1/rho = 6(a2-a1)(t-t0)(1+m)^2 / { h [ 3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn)) ] }, with m = a1/a2 (thickness ratio of the two layers), n = E1/E2 (modulus ratio), h = a1+a2 total thickness, width taken as unity, a1,a2 the expansion coefficients, t-t0 the uniform temperature rise. No Poisson ratio appears.
findings.evidence_quote: the following general equation for the curvature of a bi-metal strip will be obtained,  [eq.(4) follows; transcribed by me from the page image because the OCR of the equation is garbled]

findings.claim: AGREEMENT WITH THE PROJECT. The project's f(m,n) is algebraically identical to Timoshenko's printed eq.(4): the Lean definition copies the same expression (with the 1/h factor folded in). I also re-derived the strip curvature from Timoshenko's own equilibrium conditions (axial forces equal, moment Ph/2 = M1+M2, equal strain at the interface) with sympy; it matches the printed f with residual exactly 0. R&M 2009 eq.2.6 and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) (with M for E) are the same function (see below).

CONVENTIONS. Timoshenko uses m = a1/a2 and n = E1/E2 with layer 2 the high-expansion layer on the convex side; Reyssat & Mahadevan use m = h_p/h_a and n = E_p/E_a (passive/active) with alpha = alpha_a - alpha_p. f(m,n) = f(1/m,1/n) exactly (sympy residual 0), so swapping which layer is called 1 changes nothing; only the sign of curvature depends on which layer expands more.
findings.source: https://archive.org/download/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3.pdf (PDF pages 41-50 = journal pp.233-242; doi 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233) ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2838359/ (doi 10.1098/rsif.2009.0184); equation images https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/1901/2838359/bf169d9f0304/rsif20090184e5.jpg and .../f04e37537981/rsif20090184e6.jpg ; D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-bilayer-theory-verified/verify_bilayer.py (output verify_bilayer_out.json)

findings.claim: STATED ASSUMPTIONS (Timoshenko 1925). Narrow strip of unit width; cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the curved axis (Euler-Bernoulli, no shear deformation); uniform temperature; difference of expansion coefficients constant; perfect weld; no friction at supports; isotropic layers implicit (one E and one alpha per layer). He calls these 'ideal conditions' and says they are 'not far removed from real conditions'. No explicit thin-layer or small-strain statement is made; the algebra is linear in strain.
findings.value: narrow strip; plane sections; constant delta-alpha; perfect bond
findings.evidence_quote: it was assumed that the difference in the coefficients of expansion remained constant during heating, that the friction at the supports could be neglected and that the width of the strip could be considered as being very small.

findings.claim: Timoshenko's own plane-section assumption, page 234.
findings.evidence_quote: The following analysis has been made on the assumption that cross-sections of the strip originally plane and perpendicular to the axis remain plane during bending and become perpendicular to the curved axis of the strip.

findings.claim: TIMOSHENKO'S OWN REMARK ON MODULUS RATIO IS NARROWER THAN 'THE MODULUS RATIO DROPS OUT'. He prints the special case m=1: 1/rho = 24(a2-a1)(t-t0)/[h(14+n+1/n)] (eq.5), = (3/2)(..)/h at n=1 (eq.6), = (48/33)(..)/h at n=1/2 or 2 (eq.7), and concludes n has no substantial effect because (6) and (7) differ by about 3 percent. That holds only for n within 1/2..2 at equal thickness. At m=1, n=10 the coefficient is 0.9959, 33.6 percent below the ceiling. The project's statement (modulus ratio drops out) is correct only at the optimum m^2 n = 1; Timoshenko does not claim more. My sympy/numpy check reproduces 24/(14+n+1/n), 3/2, 48/33 and the 3.03 percent difference.
findings.evidence_quote: The difference between (6) and (7) is only about 3 per cent.

findings.claim: THE CEILING 3/2 AND THE OPTIMUM m^2 n = 1 ARE NOT STATED IN TIMOSHENKO 1925. I searched the OCR of the whole article (pp.233-255) for optimum, maximum, minimum, greatest; 'maximum' appears only for stresses. So the ceiling and optimum are the project's derivation (Lean-checked), not a quotation of Timoshenko. (OCR of equations is imperfect, so a printed statement in an equation line could have been missed.) Independent proof of mine: 3/2 - f = 3(m^2 n - 1)^2 / (2 (m^4 n^2 + 4 m^3 n + 6 m^2 n + 4 m n + 1)), which is >= 0 with equality iff m^2 n = 1 (sympy factorisation). Brute-force over 2,404,601 (m,n) points on 1e-3..1e3 gives max f = 1.5000000000000002; argmax m = n^-1/2 for n = 0.1...100.

PHYSICAL MEANING OF THE OPTIMUM (own identity). m^2 n = 1 is the same as E1 a1^2 = E2 a2^2, i.e. the stiffness-weighted first moment about the interface vanishes: the interface is the neutral axis of the unloaded composite. That is why at the optimum the curvature depends only on the first moment of the eigenstrain and not on n, and (finding below) why the response-time curve is identical for n=1 and n=10.

PLANE STRESS / PLANE STRAIN IN THE ORIGINAL. Timoshenko treats the wide plate himself (section 4, p.242): uniform heating bends a plate into a sphere (equal curvatures), which needs only E -> E/(1-sigma) in each layer (sigma = Poisson ratio, equal for both materials). The final equations contain only the ratio of moduli, so eq.(4) and (6) 'remain without any change'. So the plate formula is NOT E/(1-nu^2); it is the biaxial modulus E/(1-nu) and the coefficient f is unchanged. He also states a limit: the small-deflection plate result holds while the deflection is less than about half the plate thickness; beyond that the mid-surface strain (stretching) matters.
findings.value: E -> E/(1-sigma); f unchanged; valid for sag < h/2
findings.source: https://archive.org/download/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3.pdf (PDF pages 41-50 = journal pp.233-242; doi 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233) (journal p.242, PDF page 50)
findings.evidence_quote: If the deflections are small, say less than a half of the thickness of the plate, this strain in the middle surface of the plate can be neglected without any essential error

findings.claim: WHERE E/(1-nu^2) DOES ENTER (own derivation, sympy, linear 3-D elasticity, plane stress through thickness). If a wide plate is forced to a CYLINDER (curvature in one direction only, as happens beyond the sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation), the layers see plane-strain-like constraint: effective modulus E/(1-nu^2) and effective eigenstrain (1+nu)*eps. For equal Poisson ratio in both layers the cylinder curvature is exactly (1+nu) times the strip (Timoshenko) curvature, independent of m and n; the sphere is exactly 1.0 times. For nu = 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.5 the factor is 1.30, 1.35, 1.40, 1.50. If the layers have different nu (0.35 stiff, 0.49 soft, n=10, m=1) the factor is 1.56 relative to the beam value. The ceiling 3/2 therefore becomes (1+nu)*3/2 for a wide cylindrically-curved plate (2.25 at nu=0.5), not a violation but a different regime.
findings.value: kappa_cyl/kappa_beam = 1+nu (equal nu); sphere/beam = 1; unequal nu example 1.56

findings.claim: INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF (1+nu) 1: Pezzulla et al. minimise a plate energy for a sheet with dome-like natural curvature in the large-stretch (isometric) limit and obtain L+N = kappa_o(1+nu) with Gaussian curvature K=0, where kappa_o is the curvature of the beam cut from the sheet; for nu=1/2 the mean curvature is 3/4 kappa_o. A cylinder (N=0) therefore has L=(1+nu)kappa_o. Experiments (PVS bilayer disks) and neo-Hookean finite-element runs on several shapes collapse onto the three-fourths law.
findings.evidence_quote: The minimization gives L + N = κo(1 + ν) and K = 0, a solution solely in terms of the principal invariants of the curvature tensor

findings.claim: INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF (1+nu) 2: Alben's discrete bilayer model (equal layers of thickness h, equal moduli, lattice Poisson ratio nu=1/3) gives an analytic cylindrical state eps_x = eps_a/2, eps_y = 0, kappa = eps_a/h, and his mesh simulation reports curvature 8.5-10.5 against 10. Minimising his printed energy eq.(7) with sympy gives kappa = 4 Cs eps_a h/(8Cb+3Cs h^2), which equals eps_a/h for his constants (Cs h^2 = 8 Cb). Timoshenko's beam value for equal layers is 0.75 eps_a/h, and (1+nu)*0.75 = (4/3)*0.75 = 1.0, so his cylinder equals (1+nu) times the beam value exactly. In the thin-membrane limit (Cb->0) the same formula gives (4/3) eps_a/h.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.1007 (S. Alben, Bending of bilayers with general initial shapes; NOT the Nano Letters paper) ; D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-bilayer-theory-verified/alben_eq7_check.py
findings.evidence_quote: For the parameters in this simulation, ϵx = 0.05; ϵy = 0; κ = 10.

findings.claim: WHEN IS A PRINTED STRIP 'NARROW'? Three independent criteria all scale as sqrt(h/kappa) and agree within a factor of about 2 on the plate diameter D above which the strip value fails: (i) Timoshenko p.242 sag kappa D^2/8 < h/2 gives D < 2.0 sqrt(h/kappa); (ii) Freund-Floro-Chason's linearity limit S = K = kappa R^2/(4 h_s) < 0.3 gives D < 2.19 sqrt(h/kappa); (iii) Pezzulla's sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation for a disk gives R_c = 2.112 sqrt(h/kappa), D_c = 4.22 sqrt(h/kappa) (sag 2.2 h at bifurcation). Holmes' review states the same scaling kappa_n ~ h/l^2. At the optimum kappa=1.5 eps/h, so sqrt(h/kappa)=h/sqrt(1.5 eps): 2.3-29 mm over the table (h 0.4-1.6 mm, eps 0.2-2 %), confirming the earlier agent's range; Pezzulla critical disk diameters are 9.8-123 mm over the same grid.

findings.claim: PRIOR GAP CLOSED, WITH A CAVEAT: spec-bilayer-physics could not retrieve the numerical prefactor of the sphere-to-cylinder transition. Pezzulla eq.(6) gives it for convex disks: kappa_ob (curvature scaled by 1/h) = sqrt((20+14*sqrt2)/27) * gamma^2 = 1.2141 gamma^2, gamma = h/S, shape factor S = ((2/9) * integral r^4 dA / A)^(1/4); for a disk S = (2/27)^(1/4) R = 0.5217 R. I read the equation from the PDF text layer (symbols partly garbled) and recomputed the constants; I could not compare against the figure. For a long strip the shape factor is dominated by the LENGTH (L^4/360 for L>>w), so eq.(6) is a sphere-vs-cylinder criterion for a convex sheet, not a strip-width criterion. findings.claim: STONEY 1909, as printed. A steel rule (102 mm long, 12 mm wide, 0.32 mm thick) is coated with nickel of thickness t on one side. Taking moments gives neutral axis at b = (2/3)d, then P t = (1/6) E d^2 / r, and with r = l^2/(8z): P = (4/3) E d^2 z /(t l^2) (eq.1), for a very thin film. A correction for finite film thickness (assuming film and rule have the same modulus) gives P = (4/3) E (d^2 + t d) z /(t l^2) (eq.2). E is the plain Young's modulus (no Poisson ratio); the formula is a one-way strip result. Own check: sympy reproduces eq.(1) from P t = E d^2/(6r).
findings.value: P = E d^2/(6 r t) (thin film, strip); 1/r = 6 P t/(E d^2)
findings.evidence_quote: This equation is only true when the film of nickel is very thin;

findings.claim: STONEY'S STATED LIMITS. Film 'very thin'; thickness of the rule neglected against r in the first derivation; the thick-film correction assumes the film has the same modulus as the substrate; no Poisson ratio, no plane strain, no nonlinear range. The modern equibiaxial form sigma_f = E_s h_s^2 kappa/(6(1-nu_s) h_f) is a later restatement for plates (quoted in Injeti et al.), not Stoney's printed equation.
findings.value: thin film, uniaxial E; modern form uses 1/(1-nu)
findings.evidence_quote: neglecting the thickness of the rule, which is small in comparison with r

findings.claim: TIMOSHENKO REDUCES TO STONEY FOR A THIN FILM. Taking a1 -> 0 in kappa = eps f/(a1+a2): kappa -> 6 eps (E1/E2)(a1/a2)/a2, which is Stoney's 1/r = 6 P t/(E d^2) with P = E_film*eps (sympy limit = 6). So Stoney's equation is the thin-film limit of the project's f; the project's f is exact in thickness ratio within beam theory, so Stoney's 'film must be thin' limit does not apply to it.
findings.value: lim f/(6 m n) = 1 as m->0

findings.claim: FREUND-FLORO-CHASON (1999) eq.(6), the plate generalisation of Stoney for arbitrary thickness and modulus ratio, is Timoshenko's f: kappa = (6 eps_m/h_s) h m [ (1+h) / (1 + h m (4+6h+4h^2) + h^4 m^2) ], h = h_f/h_s, m = M_f/M_s with biaxial modulus M = E/(1-nu). Substituting h = a1/a2, m = E1/E2 gives Timoshenko's kappa with residual exactly 0 (sympy). The difference between the two is therefore only (a) M instead of E and (b) circular plate versus narrow strip.
findings.value: FFC eq.(6) = Timoshenko eq.(4) with E -> E/(1-nu)

findings.claim: FFC STATED ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS (the Stoney formula's six assumptions): (i) thicknesses small against lateral size; (ii) film much thinner than substrate; (iii) homogeneous, isotropic, linear-elastic substrate and isotropic film; (iv) edge effects inconsequential, quantities uniform in the plane; (v) no through-thickness stress; (vi) infinitesimal strains and rotations. They relax (ii) and (vi). Stoney with equal moduli at h_f/h_s = 0.1 is 'in error by 30 percent' (printed); my evaluation of their eq.(6) gives kappa/kappa_Stoney = 0.7513 = 1/(1+h)^3, i.e. Stoney overestimates by 33.1 percent. Nonlinear (rotation-stretching) effects set in for normalised mismatch strain S = (3/2) eps R^2 h_f M_f/(h_s^3 M_s) above roughly 0.3; the nonlinear law is S = K[1+(1-nu_s)K^2], K = R^2 kappa/(4 h_s). For R/h_s=100, h_f/h_s=0.01, equal moduli, S=0.3 corresponds to eps_m about 0.002.
findings.value: S_crit ~ 0.3; Stoney error 30 % (printed) / 33.1 % (computed) at m=1, h=0.1

findings.evidence_quote: nonlinear effects arise for normalized mismatch strain in excess of roughly 0.3.

findings.claim: FREUND 2000 (J. Mech. Phys. Solids 48, 1159) ITSELF WAS NOT READ: paywalled, no open copy found; Crossref confirms the DOI and Elsevier licence only. What I report about 'Freund on bilayer plates' comes from the 1999 companion paper by the same author (open preprint) and from search-result summaries of the 2000 abstract (nonlinear range, S about 0.3, bifurcation from axisymmetric to asymmetric). Treat the 2000 paper's content as second-hand.

REYSSAT & MAHADEVAN 2009: eq.(2.5) is delta-kappa = alpha delta-phi f(m,n)/h and eq.(2.6) is f(m,n) = 6(1+m)^2/[3(1+m)^2+(1+mn)(m^2+1/(mn))] exactly as Timoshenko, with m = h_p/h_a, n = E_p/E_a, total h = h_p+h_a, linear hygrometric expansion coefficients assumed independent of humidity. I read the equation images (rsif20090184e5.jpg, e6.jpg), which closes the earlier agent's gap that the printed equations were images not captured. They say f(m,n)=0 as n -> 0 or infinity, and that for m=1 f varies by under 10 percent for n in 0.3-3.5 (my numbers: f(1,0.3)=1.361, f(1,3.5)=1.349, 9.3 and 10.0 percent below f(1,1) and the ceiling respectively: agreement within rounding) and under 20 percent for n 0.3-5 (computed 16.7 percent).
findings.evidence_quote: we adapt the theory of bimetallic thermostats to hygrometry sensors (Timoshenko 1925), as the actuation mechanism of pine cone scales relies on the same principle, with humidity replacing temperature.

findings.claim: PINE CONE CHECK. R&M take m about 1, n about 5 (moduli from Dawson et al. 1997) and state f(m,n) is about 1.3; the printed formula gives f(1,5) = 1.25 (4 percent lower than the rounded 1.3). Their text says the strain of the active cells along the axis is alpha = 0.001 per percent relative humidity, with no significant radial strain (an extreme natural case of anisotropic swelling).
findings.evidence_quote: the thickness ratio m = hp/ha ≃ 1, while the length of the active zone La ≃ 10ha

findings.claim: DIFFUSION-LIMITED ACTUATION TIME, original statement. R&M: imbibition time scale tau ~ h^2/D; for molecular pores D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s, active-layer thickness 1 mm gives tau ~ 1000 s; with a bottleneck of size l_b, tau ~ h_a l_b/D. Their measured pine-scale fits are sub-quadratic: drying tau = 96 h_a^1.5 min, wetting tau = 29 h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm), which they attribute to strong strains (up to 20 percent) coupled to transport and a bottleneck. So h^2/D is a scaling, not a law, even in the source.
findings.value: tau~h^2/D; D~1e-9 m^2/s -> ~1000 s at 1 mm; exponents 1.3-1.5 measured
findings.evidence_quote: For molecular pores, D ∼ 10−9 m2 s−1, the thickness of the active layer ha ∼ 1 mm and τ = ha2/D ∼ 1000 s

findings.claim: MEASURED D FOR DENSE PRINTABLE POLYMERS (re-checked). Aniskevich et al. Table 3 (1.75-2.8 mm filament cylinders, up to 97 percent RH): D = 0.001 (Nylon), 0.00245 (Antero), 0.00247 (CPE), 0.00335 (PET-G), 0.00399 (Ultem), 0.00472 (PC), 0.00782 (PLA LAVA), 0.0151 (PLA T-W) mm^2/h, with time to reach 80 percent of equilibrium moisture 360 h (Nylon), 92 h (PC), 27 h (PLA T-W) and up to 550 h (Koltron). This confirms the earlier agent's range 0.001-0.0151 mm^2/h. Several grades have concentration-dependent D, so these are order-of-magnitude inputs, and none is a Formlabs material.

CURVATURE RESPONSE TIME (own calculation, linear bilayer with a diffusing eigenstrain). Active layer (thickness a) exposed on its free face only, bonded face sealed, eigenstrain proportional to local concentration. Curvature reaches 63 percent at D t/a^2 = 0.198, 90 percent at 0.724, 99 percent at 1.67, never overshoots; mass uptake reaches 90 percent at 0.861; the slowest mode is 4/pi^2 = 0.405. At the optimum m^2 n = 1 the normalised curve is identical for n=1 and n=10 (interface = neutral axis); for n=3, m=1 it is faster (t90 = 0.542). In real units with measured D (0.0151-0.001 mm^2/h): a = 0.2 mm -> t90 = 1.9-29 h; a = 0.4 mm -> 7.7-116 h; a = 0.8 mm -> 31-463 h. This agrees with the earlier agent's h^2/D table (0.4 mm: 10.6-160 h) after the factor 0.72.
findings.confidence: medium (model assumes sealed bond face, Fickian constant D)

findings.claim: KINETICS AND STIFFNESS ARE COUPLED AT THE OPTIMUM (own consequence of m = n^-1/2). If the swelling layer is the STIFF one (n = E_active/E_passive > 1) the optimum makes it the thin one (n=10: active = 24 percent of total thickness, 0.19 mm of 0.8 mm), which is also the fast layer. If the swelling layer is the SOFT one (n < 1, hydrogel or elastomer) the optimum makes it the thick one (n = 0.1: active = 76 percent of total), and the t ~ a^2/D penalty grows. This matters for the Flexible 80A (active, soft) against rigid (passive) pairing considered by the earlier agents.

ASSUMPTION AUDIT 1, NARROW VS WIDE (sizes). A printed strip is 'narrow' only if its width is below roughly 2-4 sqrt(h/kappa) (previous finding). Wider, three things change: it stays spherical (curvature = beam value, Timoshenko p.242) while the sag is below about h/2; then it bifurcates to a cylinder along the long side whose curvature is (1+nu) times the beam value, 30-50 percent more for nu 0.3-0.5 (own derivation, Pezzulla, Alben), and up to 1.56 for dissimilar Poisson ratios (0.35 vs 0.49 example). A cylinder also means the strip cannot curve across its width (relevant to a doubly curved architectural panel).

ASSUMPTION AUDIT 2, END ZONES AND THE JOINT. Timoshenko says the shear (and, for different moduli, normal) stresses at the ends of the strip cannot be found elementarily, are 'local' within a distance of the order of the thickness, and 'may be of the same order' as the normal stresses, so the bond between two materials matters. Size for a 40 mm strip at h = 0.8 mm: 2 x 0.8/40 = 4 percent of the length is end zone (own arithmetic). Two separately printed layers bonded with adhesive add a third layer that Timoshenko's two-layer theory does not contain; I did not quantify it.
findings.value: end zone ~ h each end; ~4 % of a 40 mm strip at h=0.8 mm
findings.source: https://archive.org/download/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3.pdf (PDF pages 41-50 = journal pp.233-242; doi 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233) (journal p.238, PDF page 46)
findings.evidence_quote: they are of “local” type and are concentrated near the ends of the strip along a distance, the magnitude of which is of the same order as the thickness h of the strip.

findings.claim: ASSUMPTION AUDIT 3, ANISOTROPY OF PRINTED PARTS (what is published). Formlabs' Nylon 12 powder datasheet gives one tensile modulus (1850 MPa) but elongation at break 11 percent in X/Y and 6 percent in Z; its Nylon 11 CF powder gives tensile modulus 5.3 / 2.8 / 1.6 GPa for X / Y / Z (3.3x between X and Z). For SLA the only source found is Formlabs' own blog test (Form 2, Clear Resin, ASTM D638 Type IV bars at 15-degree build angles), which says strength and Young's modulus stay 'roughly constant' with build angle: SLA parts are 'isotropic for all intents and purposes', but one printer, one resin, vendor-authored. No source gives anisotropy of HYGROSCOPIC SWELLING in a printed part. In beam theory only the modulus and swelling strain along the strip axis enter, so for a strip whose axis lies in the build plane the Z properties do not matter; off-axis raster or fibre orientation adds bend-twist coupling (the Lean file's axial/shear strain relations) that I did not size because the in-plane shear modulus is unknown.
findings.value: Nylon 11 CF E = 5.3/2.8/1.6 GPa (X/Y/Z); Nylon 12 elongation 11/6 %
findings.evidence_quote: Tensile Modulus | 5.3 GPa | 2.8 GPa | 1.6 GPa

findings.claim: SIZE OF AN ANISOTROPY OR WET-STIFFNESS ERROR IN THE MODULUS RATIO (own calculation). Because f is flat at its optimum, misjudging n costs little: design for m = n0^-1/2 and the true n is 2x or 0.5x n0 -> f is 2.2-3.0 percent below 3/2 (n0 = 10 ... 1); 3.3x or 0.3x -> 6.8-9.3 percent. Moisture softening of only the active layer to 65 percent of dry modulus (the earlier record's Grey V5 figure, not rechecked) costs 0.9-1.2 percent; to 50 percent, 2.2-3.0 percent; to 30 percent, 6.9-9.3 percent. Formlabs' Flexible 80A V2 datasheet shows -26 Shore A points after one day in deionized water, so softening is real for that resin. So the modulus ratio is a second-order uncertainty provided the thickness ratio was chosen at the optimum.

WET, SOFT, LARGE-STRAIN (not sized). The Timoshenko/Stoney/FFC algebra is linear and small-strain. The hydrogel-type printable resins in the earlier record swell 3.5-74 percent linearly (Maennel 2020, from spec-resin-chemistry; not re-fetched here), far outside it. Pezzulla et al. had to use incompressible neo-Hookean finite elasticity with large distortions (stretch lambda up to about 1.15 in their Fig.2b) and a 1-D finite-strain beam model for kappa_o(lambda,m,n); I could not read the plotted values and did not build a finite-strain bilayer, so the size of the correction is unknown. Creep and hysteresis of printed polymers under humidity cycling were also not sized. Expect the largest departures from f for exactly the large-swelling, soft materials the project wants.
findings.evidence_quote: using a Neo-Hookean incompressible material model [21] implemented in the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics

findings.claim: ARMON ET AL. 2011 (Science 333, 1726): ONLY THE ABSTRACT COULD BE READ. Full text is behind a 403 and not in Europe PMC or arXiv. Abstract (Europe PMC): Bauhinia seed pod valves turn from flat to helical; strips cut from tissue and from composite elastic materials show helical configurations with sharp transitions; modelled by 'incompatible elasticity' as a thin strip with a flat intrinsic metric and saddle-like intrinsic curvature. I therefore cannot print the equation, its stated assumptions (thin, small strain, isotropy) or the dimensionless width parameter from the original. From a secondary source: Pezzulla et al. cite Armon for approximate expressions of the natural metric and curvature of a pre-stretched bilayer. Armon et al. 2014 (Soft Matter, abstract only) add 'dimensionless parameters' and 'quantitative predictions for the twisted-to-helical transition'. The earlier agent's w*sqrt(kappa0/t) and its limits (from a search summary) remain unverified by me.
findings.confidence: high (that I could not read it)
findings.evidence_quote: we modeled the pod as a thin strip with a flat intrinsic metric and a saddle-like intrinsic curvature.

findings.claim: ALBEN, BALAKRISNAN & SMELA 2011 (Nano Lett. 11, 2280): ONLY THE ABSTRACT COULD BE READ (not open). Claim: for thin rectangular bilayers with one isotropically strained layer, bending prefers the long edge because doubly curved regions at the curled edges lower the energy; the energy difference between 'spiral' and 'cigar' shapes grows with aspect ratio. It is consistent with Pezzulla's 'longest length' rule and with Alben's separate arXiv paper (not the Nano Letters paper), but I did not see the paper's equations or assumptions.
findings.confidence: high (that I could not read it)
findings.evidence_quote: We find that the bending direction is determined by the existence of doubly curved regions at the curled edges, which lower the energy.

findings.claim: DESIGN CONSEQUENCE OF THE BIFURCATION FOR STEERING: a wide isotropic bilayer always rolls along its long side (Pezzulla: bending along the longest length when several symmetry planes exist; Alben 2011 abstract: long edge), so a printed panel that must curl across its short side needs anisotropic swelling or stiffness (print path or fibre orientation) or slits, not just a different aspect ratio. This restates the earlier agent's point (e) with two primary-text confirmations.
findings.value: isotropic wide sheet bends along its longest length
findings.evidence_quote: If multiple planes of reflection symmetry exist for a particular shape, bending will occur along the longest length of the disk

findings.claim: DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN FORMLABS DOCUMENTS (relevant to 'stock resins gain under 1 percent in water'). Formlabs' Flexible 80A Resin V2 datasheet (ASTM D471 slabs, wiped dry) lists deionized water, 1 day: -26 Shore A, +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume; 1 week: +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume. Formlabs' solvent-compatibility page (1 cm cube, 24 h, parsed by the earlier agent from saved HTML, which I re-read) lists a row 'Flexible 80A Resin' (no V2; separate rows exist for Elastic 50A V1 and V2) with water 0.7 percent. spec-resin-chemistry ('under 1 percent for every current resin') and spec-formlabs-materials (+8 percent) are each faithful to one Formlabs source. Sibling reports of this programme (bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json, bm-formlabs-all-resins.json; not independently verified by me) read the 0.7 percent row as the OLDER formulation (its IPA value 11.7 percent matches the V1 sheet), and bm-diffusion-kinetics.json argues the two cannot be the same resin because D >= 6.3e-12 m^2/s would give about 3.8 percent in a 1 cm cube at 24 h. I therefore agree that the project-record sentence is true for the cube table but wrong for Flexible 80A V2, with the residual doubt that no V2 cube value was measured. If that sibling inversion is right (D about 9.3e-12 m^2/s = 0.0335 mm^2/h for an ASSUMED 2 mm slab), my t90 = 0.724 a^2/D gives 0.86 h (a = 0.2 mm), 3.5 h (0.4 mm), 13.8 h (0.8 mm): hours, not days, for that one resin.
findings.value: 0.7 % (cube, 24 h, older row) vs +8 % mass / +3 % volume (D471, 1 day, V2 TDS)
findings.confidence: high (both numbers exist), medium (V1 vs V2 reading, from sibling reports)
findings.evidence_quote: Deionized Water | 1 day | -26 | +8% | +3% | 94% | 89%

findings.claim: NO WATER DIFFUSIVITY FOR ANY FORMLABS OR OTHER VAT-PHOTOPOLYMER RESIN WAS FOUND, again. A second search (Europe PMC, web) found only saturation uptakes and a paper that cites ISO 62's option to fit D without reporting values; the epoxy-SLA literature calls uptake non-Fickian. The earlier gap stands, so every real-unit time above uses the FDM filament D as a bracket, not a measurement of the project's material.

CONFIRMED FROM THE EARLIER FILES (spec-bilayer-physics.json): f(1,10)=0.9959 and a 34 percent loss (mine 33.6); f(1,5)=1.25; optimum m=n^-1/2 and ceiling 3/2; 0.4 mm dense-polymer times 10.6-160 h as h^2/D; filament D range; 2.3-29 mm width scale. CORRECTED OR DEEPENED: (1) 'Original Timoshenko text not read' is now read and eq.(4) matches; (2) 'R&M equations are images' now read; (3) 'Eq.3 of Rueggeberg & Burgert partly garbled' is unnecessary, the primary forms are in hand; (4) its sentence that wide sheets roll at about (1+nu) times the beam curvature is confirmed but applies only after the sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation (below that the plate is a sphere at 1.0x, per Timoshenko p.242); (5) its inference 'could be in Timoshenko 1925' about the optimum is answered: it is not; (6) the prefactor of the transition is now available for disks.

key_claims.claim: The project's f(m,n) is Timoshenko's printed eq.(4) (also R&M eq.2.6, and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) with E -> E/(1-nu)); it is a narrow-strip, linear, perfectly-bonded, plane-section result with no Poisson ratio, and Timoshenko 1925 does NOT state the ceiling 3/2 or optimum m^2 n = 1 (those are the project's derivation, here re-proved: 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(m^4n^2+4m^3n+6m^2n+4mn+1))).
key_claims.evidence_quote: the following general equation for the curvature of a bi-metal strip will be obtained,  [eq.(4) on journal p.235, transcribed from page image]

key_claims.claim: Plane stress versus plane strain: for a wide plate Timoshenko himself substitutes the biaxial modulus E/(1-nu) and f is unchanged (sphere, valid while sag < h/2). Beyond the sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation (diameter above about 4.2 sqrt(h/kappa) for a disk) the curvature becomes (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent), confirmed by my sympy derivation, Pezzulla et al. (L+N = kappa_o(1+nu)) and Alben's model. So E/(1-nu^2) matters only in that cylindrical regime, and the strip result is safe for strips narrower than about 2 sqrt(h/kappa).
key_claims.evidence_quote: It is necessary only to substitute E1/(1−σ) and E2/(1−σ) instead of E1 and E2 where σ denotes Poisson's ratio considered as equal for both materials.

key_claims.claim: Diffusion-limited actuation: tau ~ h^2/D in the original (R&M), with measured sub-quadratic fits (exponents 1.3-1.5). With the only measured D for printable dense polymers (0.001-0.0151 mm^2/h, FDM filaments, none Formlabs), my model gives a 90 percent curvature response at 0.72 a^2/D: 1.9-29 h at a = 0.2 mm, 7.7-116 h at 0.4 mm, 31-463 h at 0.8 mm. No D for any Formlabs resin exists in the sources found.
key_claims.evidence_quote: For molecular pores, D ∼ 10−9 m2 s−1, the thickness of the active layer ha ∼ 1 mm and τ = ha2/D ∼ 1000 s

key_claims.claim: Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 (JMPS) could not be read in the original (only abstracts, or a companion paper); statements about their equations, assumptions and critical values are second-hand and labelled so.
key_claims.evidence_quote: we modeled the pod as a thin strip with a flat intrinsic metric and a saddle-like intrinsic curvature.

recommendations: Keep f(m,n) and the 3/2 ceiling, but state its regime next to every curvature prediction: narrow strip (width below about 2 sqrt(h/kappa), i.e. 2-29 mm for the planned table), linear and small strain, perfectly bonded. Quote Timoshenko 1925 eq.(4) as the source of f, not of the optimum.

Cite the optimum m^2 n = 1 and the 3/2 ceiling as the project's own result (Lean plus the factorised identity 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(...)) in this report), because Timoshenko's paper does not contain them; if a reviewer asks for a printed source, none was found.

For wide architectural panels, predict the curvature with the plate model, not the strip: sphere (strip value) while the sag is below about h/2, then a cylinder along the long side at (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent). To curl across the short side, add anisotropy (print path, fibre or rib orientation) or slits.

Because kinetics scale as a^2/D and the optimum makes a soft active layer the thick one (m = n^-1/2), prefer a STIFF active layer or a thin soft one with a fast-water route; do not pair a thick soft swelling layer with a rigid passive layer if hour-scale actuation is wanted.

Close the two biggest measurement gaps with one bench step each before designing around them: (a) weigh a Flexible 80A V2 cube and a 0.4 mm strip in water over 1, 6, 24, 168 h and fit D and the saturation (resolves the 0.7 versus 8 percent conflict and supplies the missing D); (b) measure the free swelling strain of each layer separately with a ruler or calipers (the real bottleneck for testing the 20 percent claim).

For the Lean track (read-only here, so a suggestion): add (i) the neutral-axis identity E1 a1^2 = E2 a2^2 <=> m^2 n = 1, (ii) the closed form 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(...)), (iii) the invariance of f under E -> E/(1-nu) for equal nu and under m,n -> 1/m,1/n, and (iv) the (1+nu) cylinder theorem; all four were proved symbolically here.
Retrieve Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 through a library or the authors' pages before any partner document cites their equations or critical widths.

Optica's own copy of Timoshenko 1925: the site served a bot-check captcha page to an automated fetch; I did not try to defeat it and used the Internet Archive scan of the same journal issue instead. Water diffusion coefficient or hygroscopic expansion coefficient for any Formlabs resin or powder: searched again (Europe PMC, web), nothing found; the FDM filament values are brackets only.

Any measurement of anisotropy of hygroscopic swelling (not stiffness) in a printed polymer part; no value for in-plane shear modulus of printed layers, so bend-twist coupling for off-axis print paths was not sized.

A numerical size for the large-strain (hydrogel, 3.5-74 percent swelling) correction to the linear Timoshenko result: Pezzulla's plotted values could not be read and I did not build a finite-strain bilayer model.

Any quantitative treatment of an adhesive or interfacial layer between two separately printed halves, of creep or hysteresis in printed polymers under humidity cycling, or of the peel/shear stress at the strip ends beyond Timoshenko's qualitative statement.

A V2 cube-test value for Flexible 80A water uptake: sibling reports read the 0.7 percent cube row as the older formulation and the V2 datasheet gives +8 percent mass (slab), but no measurement of V2 in the cube test or of its slab thickness exists in the sources I saw; the V1/V2 reading is therefore second-hand and a bench weighing would settle it.
